children: Launched in 2020 under Atmanirbhar Bharat, the Production-linked Incentive (PLI) programme seeks to strengthen domestic manufacturing, promote import substitution and boost exports through targeted incentives across 14 strategic sectors, raising manufacturing’s GDP share from around 13 per cent towards the 25 per cent target.

Five years on, the NITI Aayog-IIM Ahmedabad assessment provides the first comprehensive evaluation of the programme, identifying its achievements, persistent structural gaps and the need for differentiated, sector-specific policy interventions.

The assessment identifies eight broad weaknesses: uneven sectoral performance, slow incentive disbursement, shallow domestic value-addition, upstream supply-chain deficiencies, inadequate demand creation, limited MSME participation, weak outcome monitoring and rigid scheme design.

This assessment warrants examining whether PLI has delivered on its core objectives, import substitution, manufacturing competitiveness, economic growth and employment, and addressed capability gaps in emerging industries to position India as a globally competitive manufacturing hub. The following cases illustrate its successes and persisting policy gaps.
The policy gaps

Before start, let us decode how the PLI scheme provides financial incentives to eligible manufacturers for achieving incremental production or sales over a defined base year. Its design rests on four pillars: eligibility, tenure, incentive amount and calculation criteria, albeit differentiated by parameters such as sales revenue, net worth, strategic importance, technological requirements, financial performance and value-chain position.

However, the ACC battery experience illustrates the risks of prioritising financial commitments over technological readiness. For example, in the first round, allocations went to Rajesh Exports, Ola Electric, Hyundai Global Motors and Reliance, while established battery manufacturers such as Exide Industries and Amara Raja were not selected. Eligibility criteria did not adequately emphasise prior cell-manufacturing experience or technology-transfer partnerships.

Consequently, beneficiaries encountered technological and supply-chain constraints, including dependence on imported machinery, critical minerals and technical expertise, delaying commissioning and capacity creation. The experience highlights the need to make technological competence, execution capabilities and credible technology partnerships integral to beneficiary selection in strategically important industries.

The solar PV PLI scheme similarly illustrates the limits of incentive-led capacity expansion amid supply-chain weaknesses. By September 2026, India’s module assembly capacity had reached 175 GW, while upstream capacities remained limited, with polysilicon below 4GW and ingots and wafers below 10GW. These stages demand specialised technology, substantial capital, imported machinery and competitively priced, uninterrupted electricity. High energy costs further undermine domestic competitiveness against established global manufacturers. Module-level incentives alone cannot bridge these capability gaps.
The priority must shift towards building an integrated solar manufacturing ecosystem, strengthening upstream production rather than merely expanding downstream assembly.
Success stories

The PLI scheme’s visible benefits to certain sectors, for example, food processing offers a contrasting example of how production incentives, supported by an enabling ecosystem, can generate wider economic gains. Potato processing into frozen French fries illustrates the potential to convert perishable agricultural produce, including varieties unsuitable for fresh consumption, into higher-value, exportable products. India now exports processed frozen fries, wedges and chips (HSN-200410) worth ₹2,500 crore to almost 90 countries of the world.

Similarly, fruit pulping, concentrates and beverages (HSN-200799, 220299) extend shelf life, reduce post-harvest losses and create assured markets for farmers. This ensured vital domestic availability to consumers and brought ₹1,500 crore of exports as well. The combination of processing facilities, cold chains, collection centres and Mega Food Parks strengthens farm-to-factory linkages, enabling value addition closer to production centres.

More specifically, results are reflected in the wider sectoral performance: PLI-supported investments have added approximately 34 lakh tonnes of annual processing capacity and generated over 3.3 lakh direct and indirect jobs. Meanwhile, 25 Mega Food Parks are operational, providing shared infrastructure for storage, processing and distribution. The experience demonstrates that incentives work better when they complement existing agricultural strengths and address supply-chain bottlenecks.

Likewise, India’s dependence on imported Key Starting Materials (KSMs), Drug Intermediates (DIs) and Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs), particularly from China, exposed vulnerabilities in its pharmaceutical supply chain despite its global leadership in generic medicines. The bulk-drug PLI scheme sought to reverse this dependence by incentivising domestic manufacturing of critical inputs.

A notable success is Penicillin-G (HSN-294110), a critical fermentation-based input for antibiotic production. Domestic production has also commenced for Clavulanic Acid, Rifampicin, Levofloxacin and Norfloxacin. Collectively, the PLI-supported bulk-drug ecosystem has established approximately 55,000 tonnes of annual capacity across 26 critical products.

More significantly, India’s bulk-drug trade position shifted from a ₹1,930-crore deficit in FY22 to a ₹2,280-crore surplus in FY25. This marks a significant movement towards import substitution, supply-chain resilience and domestic technological capabilities.
Way forward

Overcoming these limitations requires a shift from uniform incentives to a differentiated, capability-driven industrial policy. As the assessment highlights, eligibility must prioritise technological readiness, domestic value addition and execution capabilities over investment commitments alone. Incentives should extend beyond final assembly to critical components, raw materials, KSMs, APIs and semiconductor inputs, strengthening backward linkages.

A ‘Banyan Tree’ strategy can provide the strategic framework: deepen domestic roots through indigenous technology and critical-input capabilities; expand global branches through diversified technology partnerships and supply networks; and reach multiple markets through FTAs and export diversification. Domestic demand must provide scale, not permanent protection, making global competitiveness the ultimate test of PLI support.

Correspondingly, faster disbursement, predictable guidelines and simplified compliance must restore investor confidence. MSME integration requires cluster-based support, affordable credit, common testing facilities and stronger industry linkages. Public procurement and strategic trade partnerships should stimulate demand. Finally, independent monitoring of incremental investment, productivity, exports, employment and domestic value addition must guide periodic recalibration, discontinuation of underperforming schemes and efficient fiscal resource allocation.

title: PLI scheme: Hits and misses
